prompt_free_text:
This paper studies an important and timely problem: when users access language models through black-box APIs, are they actually receiving samples from the advertised model distribution? The paper formalizes this as a two-sample hypothesis testing problem, “Model Equality Testing,” and proposes MMD-based tests with string kernels, especially a simple Hamming kernel over completions. The empirical study includes both controlled simulations against quantization, watermarking, finetuning, and model swaps, and an audit of 31 commercial endpoints serving Llama-family models. The main empirical claim is that the Hamming-kernel MMD test is sample-efficient and practically useful, and that several commercial endpoints appear statistically distinguishable from Meta’s released reference weights.

Overall, I found the paper interesting, well motivated, and potentially impactful. The problem formulation is clean and broadly useful, and the paper succeeds in connecting a practical systems/auditing question to a classical statistical testing framework. The empirical findings on commercial APIs are likely to attract substantial attention, and the release of code and data is a strong positive. At the same time, I have several concerns about the statistical framing, the interpretation of the audit results, and the extent to which the chosen kernel captures “model equality” in a meaningful sense. My view is that this is a strong paper with clear novelty and practical relevance, but it would benefit from sharper discussion of what exactly is being tested, stronger calibration/robustness evidence, and more careful interpretation of endpoint “failures.”

The strongest aspect of the paper is the problem formulation. Framing API auditing as a two-sample test between prompt-completion distributions is elegant and useful. It naturally covers both “is this the advertised model?” and “has this endpoint changed over time?” under one umbrella. This is a meaningful conceptual contribution because much prior auditing work indeed focuses on benchmark accuracy under deterministic or near-deterministic decoding, whereas many real users care about the full sampled distribution. The paper also does a good job motivating why exact equality is difficult in high-dimensional sequence spaces and why kernel methods may help by imposing a useful similarity structure.

The methodological choice of MMD is sensible. It is a standard, flexible nonparametric tool, and the paper is honest that kernel choice determines both semantics and power. I appreciated the discussion contrasting universal kernels such as one-hot or all-substrings with the non-universal but more sample-efficient Hamming kernel. This is exactly the right tradeoff to surface. The empirical result that one-hot style tests are ineffective in the sparse small-sample regime is unsurprising but important to demonstrate in this application. The paper’s emphasis on sample efficiency is also appropriate, since API auditing is constrained by cost.

The empirical evaluation is broad and generally convincing at a high level. The simulations cover several realistic distortions: quantization, watermarking, finetuning, and outright model substitution. The finding that the Hamming MMD retains power better than multinomial-style tests as completion length grows is plausible and useful. The API audit itself is the most compelling part of the paper. Testing 31 endpoints across multiple providers and models gives the work practical significance beyond a purely methodological paper. The cost estimates are also helpful and support the claim that the method is accessible to end users.

That said, my main concern is that the paper sometimes overstates what its test establishes. The null hypothesis is equality of prompt-completion distributions under a specific prompt distribution, decoding setup, output representation, and sampling protocol. This is much narrower than “which model is this API serving?” in the colloquial sense. In practice, many factors besides model weights can induce detectable differences: tokenizer/version mismatches, stop-sequence handling, hidden system prompts, safety filters, server-side prompt preprocessing, decoding implementation details, random seed handling, truncation policies, Unicode normalization, and output postprocessing. The paper acknowledges some of these possibilities in motivation, but the audit results are still presented in a way that may be read as evidence that providers are serving a different model. More precisely, the test detects a distributional difference relative to the chosen reference pipeline. That is already valuable, but the interpretation should be tightened throughout, especially in the abstract and headline claims around flagged endpoints.

Relatedly, the choice to compare API outputs to local Hugging Face inference raises a reproducibility and attribution issue. For open-weight models, “reference weights” are only one part of the inference stack. Small implementation differences can matter at temperature 1, especially over long generations. If the goal is to infer undisclosed quantization or finetuning, then the paper should more clearly separate “distribution differs from our local reference implementation” from “provider modified the underlying model.” The current wording sometimes blurs these. This is particularly important because some providers may use optimized kernels, different sampler implementations, or patched tokenizers while still honestly serving the same nominal model family.

A second major concern is calibration and false positive control in the actual audit protocol. The paper states that tests are conducted at level alpha = 0.01 using N = 10m samples, then repeated over ten samples, and endpoints are failed if the average rejection rate is at least 0.5. This repeated-testing-and-thresholding procedure is not itself a standard level-controlled hypothesis test in the usual sense. It may be a pragmatic variance reduction heuristic, but then the interpretation of a “failure” is no longer simply “rejected at level 0.01.” The paper should provide either a formal analysis of this meta-decision rule or empirical calibration under known-null endpoints. As written, it is hard to know the effective false positive rate of the endpoint-level decision. The same issue applies to combining prompt distributions with Bonferroni in Figure 1 while also using repeated runs and a majority threshold. The paper needs a clearer statistical accounting of the full decision pipeline.

More broadly, I would have liked stronger null calibration experiments. For example, when P and Q are two independent sample sets from the exact same local model and inference stack, does the empirical rejection rate match alpha across all prompt distributions and lengths? How stable is this under character-space conversion? How sensitive is calibration to finite-sample estimation of the null via simulation versus permutation? The paper mentions permutation trends in the appendix, but calibration is at least as important as power here, especially because the practical claims hinge on accusing real endpoints of deviation.

The kernel choice is both the paper’s strength and a conceptual limitation. The Hamming kernel is computationally simple and empirically powerful, but it only captures token- or character-position agreement. This means the test is highly sensitive to local lexical/syntactic shifts but may miss semantically meaningful changes that preserve surface form statistics, and conversely may flag benign formatting or tokenization differences that users may not care about. The paper does acknowledge that the Hamming MMD is only a pseudometric, but the implications deserve more discussion. In particular, if the test is intended as a user-facing auditing tool, then kernel choice should arguably be task-dependent. A code user may care about AST-level or execution-level similarity; a summarization user may care about semantic content; a dialogue user may care about style and refusal behavior. The paper briefly notes that kernels define semantics, but then largely settles on Hamming as the default. I think the paper would be stronger if it framed Hamming as one practical instantiation rather than the main answer, and perhaps included at least one semantic or embedding-based kernel baseline, even if imperfect.

The character-space testing for cross-tokenizer comparisons and API audits is another place where more nuance is needed. Character-level Hamming over long decoded strings can be brittle to small formatting differences, whitespace, Unicode normalization, or provider-specific rendering conventions. Since many APIs return text rather than tokens, this choice is understandable, but it may also inflate sensitivity to superficial differences. Some robustness checks would help: for example, normalizing whitespace, lowercasing, stripping trailing spaces, or comparing sentencepiece/token-level alignments where possible. If the flagged endpoints remain flagged under such normalizations, the claims become much stronger.

I also found the treatment of the composite null in Section 5 somewhat conservative but acceptable; however, the practical rationale could be clearer. Testing against both fp32 and fp16 references is sensible if the authors want to avoid flagging providers for standard precision differences. But the paper’s own earlier experiments show low power against fp16 differences. This creates an odd asymmetry: fp16 is treated as an acceptable null, yet the chosen test is relatively insensitive to fp16-vs-fp32 anyway. It would help to report how often the two null comparisons disagree and whether flagged endpoints are clearly separated from both references in estimated effect size, not just p-values.

The empirical results are interesting, but some claims would benefit from stronger controls. For example, the paper reports that Perplexity fails all tests and qualitatively appears lower entropy. But Perplexity is also a provider where undocumented prompt wrapping, routing, or postprocessing may plausibly occur. Similarly, Amazon Bedrock and Groq failures may reflect inference stack differences rather than model substitution or finetuning. The paper does mention that some deviations may be due to implementation choices, but the discussion section should be more explicit that the method is diagnostic, not forensic: it can detect a difference, but not identify its cause. This distinction matters a lot for responsible interpretation.

The distance-estimation results are intriguing but should be interpreted cautiously. Since the Hamming MMD is kernel-dependent and not a true metric over distributions, statements like “provider deviation is as large as swapping in GPT-3.5” are rhetorically strong but somewhat fragile. They are true only relative to this kernel, prompt distribution, and decoding setup. I would recommend softening such comparisons or at least repeating them with an additional kernel to show they are not artifacts of one representation.

There are also some experimental design choices that deserve more justification. The prompt distributions are relatively small, with m = 20 or 25 prompts, and often based on random Wikipedia continuations. This is reasonable for a proof of concept, but the paper’s framing emphasizes user-customized auditing. In that setting, prompt distribution shift is central. How sensitive are conclusions to prompt selection? The paper says it repeats over ten prompt distributions in simulation, which is good, but the API audit seems to use one prompt set per task. Given the strong practical claims, I would like to see either multiple independently sampled prompt sets for the audit or confidence intervals over prompt-set variability.

The finetuning experiment is suggestive but somewhat limited. Detecting finetuning after one epoch on 1000 examples is interesting, but the setup uses full finetuning with a specific learning rate on Llama-3 8B and evaluates on Wikipedia. It would be useful to know whether the method can detect more realistic deployment modifications such as LoRA adapters, RLHF-style preference tuning, safety tuning, or distillation. Since the paper’s motivation includes undisclosed provider modifications, these may be more representative than the chosen finetuning setup.

I also think the paper could engage more with alternatives beyond MMD. For example, classifier two-sample tests, nearest-neighbor tests, compression-based distances, or language-model-based likelihood-ratio surrogates might be competitive in sequence domains. The current baselines are mostly multinomial-style tests and alternative kernels. That is a reasonable starting point, but it leaves open whether the gains come from MMD specifically or simply from using any similarity-aware representation. A learned discriminator baseline over strings or embeddings would be informative.

On presentation, the paper is generally clear and readable. The motivation is strong, and the figures appear informative. There are a few inconsistencies in the summary counts: the abstract and introduction mention 11 out of 31 endpoints in one place and 5 out of 31 in another, while Table 1 appears to show more than five failures across task/model combinations but perhaps only five unique endpoints under some aggregation. This needs to be clarified carefully, because these numbers are central to the paper’s headline result. The distinction between endpoint-task failures and unique endpoint deviations should be made explicit everywhere.

I also noticed some minor issues in exposition. The notation sometimes conflates testing equality of conditional distributions P(.|x) and Q(.|x) with equality of the joint under prompt distribution pi; this is fine mathematically, but the practical interpretation depends heavily on pi and should be emphasized more often. The paper could also better explain how right-padding and variable-length outputs interact with the Hamming kernel, especially in character space where alignment may be less meaningful after early divergence.

In terms of significance, I think the paper makes a meaningful contribution. The problem is important, the framing is elegant, and the empirical audit is novel and practically relevant. I can imagine this work being useful to researchers, developers, and perhaps even providers themselves. My reservations are not about whether the problem matters, but about whether the current paper fully supports the strongest interpretations of its findings.

My recommendation would be positive but not without hesitation. I would support acceptance if the authors can tighten the claims and strengthen the statistical validation. In particular, the paper would be substantially improved by: first, a clearer statement that the method tests equality relative to a full reference inference pipeline, not just model weights; second, empirical calibration of the full endpoint-level decision rule, including the repeated-run majority threshold; third, robustness checks for character-space normalization and superficial formatting differences; fourth, clearer accounting of the headline failure counts; and fifth, more cautious interpretation of provider deviations as evidence of “different models” rather than “different output distributions.”

To summarize the main strengths: the paper addresses an important real-world problem; the formalization as two-sample testing is elegant; the MMD/string-kernel approach is simple and practical; the empirical study is broad; and the API audit is novel and impactful. The main weaknesses are: the interpretation of detected differences is sometimes too strong; the statistical calibration of the final audit decision is underdeveloped; the chosen kernel may capture superficial rather than user-relevant differences; and some headline claims need clarification and softening.

If I were writing an author checklist of the most important revisions, it would be: clarify what “model equality” means operationally; validate false positive control for the exact audit pipeline; add robustness analyses for text normalization and prompt-set variability; and temper causal claims about why providers differ. With those improvements, this would be a strong and influential paper.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper formulates auditing black-box LLM APIs as a two-sample hypothesis testing problem called Model Equality Testing. Given samples from a reference model and an API, it applies MMD-based kernel tests to determine whether the output distributions match. The main methodological contribution is an empirical study of kernels for this setting, with a simple Hamming/string kernel emerging as the most sample-efficient among the tested options. Simulations evaluate detection of quantization, watermarking, finetuning, and model substitution, and the method is then used to audit 31 commercial endpoints serving Llama models. The paper reports that several endpoints differ significantly from Meta reference weights, and also uses estimated MMD values as effect-size measures of distributional deviation.
strengths: Addresses an important and timely practical problem: users of black-box LLM APIs often cannot verify whether the served model matches advertised reference weights or remains stable over time.
Provides a clean and intuitive formalization of API auditing as a two-sample testing problem, which is a useful abstraction likely to stimulate further work.
The use of MMD is well motivated, and the decomposition with prompt-conditioned kernels is conceptually elegant.
Empirical evaluation is broad in scope, covering multiple distortions (quantization, watermarking, finetuning, model swaps), multiple models, and real commercial APIs.
The proposed Hamming-kernel MMD appears practically sample-efficient relative to several natural baselines, which is valuable for low-cost auditing.
The paper goes beyond binary testing by also interpreting estimated MMD as an effect-size measure and using it to compare models/providers.
Open-sourcing code and a large completion dataset improves reproducibility and practical impact.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is limited: the paper mainly adapts standard MMD two-sample testing with a hand-designed string kernel, and the strongest contribution is empirical rather than theoretical.

The chosen Hamming kernel is only a pseudometric and not characteristic/universal, so the test can systematically miss important distributional differences; this limitation is acknowledged but not deeply characterized.

The empirical validation focuses on a narrow family of prompt distributions and decoding settings, leaving uncertainty about robustness to realistic user workloads, different temperatures, top-p settings, system prompts, and longer conversational contexts.

The API audit conclusions may be confounded by implementation mismatches unrelated to provider-side model modification, such as tokenizer differences, prompt formatting, hidden system prompts, stop-sequence handling, sampling algorithm differences, or undocumented decoding defaults.

The endpoint-level decision rule based on repeating tests ten times and declaring failure when average rejection rate is at least 50% is somewhat ad hoc and not tied to a clearly analyzed operating characteristic.

The paper sometimes overinterprets detected distributional differences as evidence of provider modifications, whereas the test only establishes non-equality under the experimental protocol, not the cause of the discrepancy.
The reported practical significance of some detected deviations is not always clear, especially when MMD differences do not strongly align with downstream task accuracy.
methodological_flaws: The composite-null testing argument in Section 5 is only partially satisfactory. While rejecting only when both p-values are below alpha does control type-I error under the union null, the paper does not analyze dependence between the two tests beyond a simple inequality, nor does it justify this rule as near-optimal; more importantly, the practical interpretation of 'equal to fp32 or fp16' is underspecified because many providers may differ from both while still being faithful under other benign implementation choices.

The empirical null calibration relies on simulated draws from the reference model and, in some settings, permutation procedures. However, the paper does not provide enough evidence that finite-sample calibration remains accurate under the prompt-conditioned sampling design, repeated prompts, and character-space comparisons used in the API audit. Stronger type-I validation on the exact audit pipeline is needed.

The use of character-space Hamming distance for cross-tokenizer/provider comparisons may introduce artifacts unrelated to model distribution equality. Small formatting or whitespace differences can inflate MMD, while semantically meaningful but lexically similar changes may be underdetected. This weakens causal claims about provider-side model distortion.

The thresholding scheme for endpoint failure (average rejection rate over ten runs >= 50%) is not a standard hypothesis test and lacks a formal false-positive/false-negative analysis. This creates ambiguity about the statistical meaning of a reported endpoint 'failure.'

Power comparisons across kernels may be sensitive to kernel normalization and hyperparameter choices, yet the paper largely compares a single Hamming kernel against relatively weak or computationally mismatched baselines. This limits the strength of the claim that the chosen test is broadly superior.

The paper claims some deviations are as large as swapping in another model based on estimated MMD magnitudes, but because the Hamming MMD is not a true metric on distributions and depends strongly on prompt/task choice, such cross-comparison can be misleading if interpreted too literally.
